member.name: T:GameCore.Geometry.Aabb
member.summary: An axis-aligned bounding box, stored as its minimum and maximum corners.

remarks.para: Why a struct. Math types in gameplay code are allocated in enormous numbers — every collision query builds several. In Unity a class here would put that traffic on the managed heap and show up as periodic GC spikes, which read to a player as stutter. A readonly struct lives on the stack, costs nothing to create and cannot be aliased, which also removes the bug where two entities accidentally share one box and moving either moves both.

Why min/max instead of position and size. The Python original used a top-left corner plus a size because it was drawing into a framebuffer, where Y grows downward. Unity's 2D convention is Y-up and Unreal's is Z-up, so a "top-left plus size" box does not port: the meaning of every sign flips. Corner-to-corner is convention-neutral — is simply the smaller corner on both axes — so the same code is correct in either engine. Mixing conventions between physics and rendering is one of the great time sinks of game programming, and this sidesteps it.

member.name: T:GameCore.Geometry.Sweep
member.summary: Continuous collision detection and response for axis-aligned boxes.

remarks.para: Both Unity and Unreal ship this, and in production you should normally use theirs — Physics2D.BoxCast / Rigidbody2D.Slide in Unity, UWorld::SweepSingleByChannel and CharacterMovementComponent in Unreal. It is implemented here for two reasons that survive that fact.

First, understanding it is what lets you configure theirs correctly. Unity's Rigidbody ships with Collision Detection set to Discrete, and every project eventually files the same bug: a fast projectile passes through a thin wall. Knowing that discrete detection asks "do these overlap right now" — a question a bullet that was in front on one tick and behind on the next never answers yes to — is what turns that from a mystery into a one-setting fix.

Second, gameplay code that must be deterministic and unit-testable cannot call into either physics engine, because both are stateful, both need a live scene, and neither is bit-reproducible across platforms. Anything a replay or a test depends on has to live in code like this.

member.name: M:GameCore.Geometry.Sweep.Against(GameCore.Geometry.Aabb,System.Numerics.Vector2,GameCore.Geometry.Aabb)
member.summary: Finds when, during a motion, first touches .
member.remarks: The slab method. Treat the target as two slabs, one per axis; for each, compute when the mover enters and leaves it. The boxes overlap during the window where both slabs are entered, so contact begins at max(entryX, entryY) and ends at min(exitX, exitY). If the window starts after it ends, the mover passes by without touching.
member.returns: The hit, or null if there is no contact within this step.

member.name: M:GameCore.Geometry.Sweep.MoveAndSlide(GameCore.Geometry.Aabb,System.Numerics.Vector2,System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{GameCore.Geometry.Aabb},System.Collections.Generic.List{GameCore.Geometry.SweepHit},System.Int32,System.Single)
member.summary: Moves as far as possible along , sliding along whatever is struck, and returns the motion actually performed.
member.param: Attempted motion for this step, in world units.
Receives the contacts encountered, in order.
Cap on resolution passes. Sliding off one surface can push into another — an inside corner needs two in a single step — and the cap stops a wedge-shaped dead end from looping forever.

Gap left at the contact point, in world units, not as a fraction of the step. Landing exactly on a surface means the next step starts flush against it, and floating point then decides at random whether that counts as touching, which shows up as an entity flickering between grounded and airborne. Expressing it as a fraction is a trap: the standoff would scale with speed, so a bullet stops visibly short of the wall it hit while a slow walker is left touching it.
member.remarks: Stopping dead on contact makes a game feel like it is made of glue: brush a wall while running diagonally and you halt instead of continuing along it. Sliding keeps the component of motion parallel to the surface and discards only the component heading into it.

member.name: T:GameCore.Input.ActionState
member.summary: Tracks which named actions are held, and which changed on this tick.

remarks.para: Gameplay needs three different questions answered about a button, and conflating them is a rich source of bugs: is it held (walking), was it just pressed (jumping, which must fire exactly once), and was it just released (variable-height jumps, charged attacks). Only the first is observable from hardware; the other two are derived by comparing this tick against the last, so something must own that history.

The Unity trap this exists for. Input.GetKeyDown and the new Input System's WasPressedThisFrame are keyed to the render frame. FixedUpdate does not run once per frame — it runs zero, one or several times, driven by the same accumulator as . So reading GetKeyDown inside FixedUpdate is doubly broken: a press can be missed entirely when a frame runs no fixed ticks, and can fire several times when a frame runs several. The documented fix is to sample input in Update and consume it in FixedUpdate — which means latching it somewhere, which is this class.

The second trap: losing a tap shorter than one tick. At 60 Hz a tick is 16 ms; a fast player, or a 1000 Hz gaming mouse, can press and release inside that window. Comparing before/after snapshots shows the button down at neither end and the input silently vanishes. Presses are therefore latched when they arrive and cleared only when consumed, so a press is never dropped.

Actions are named strings rather than key codes so gameplay talks about "Jump" rather than "Space". That indirection is what makes rebinding, gamepads and replay files possible without touching gameplay code, and it is the same idea as Unreal's Enhanced Input actions or Unity's Input Actions.

member.name: T:GameCore.Random.Pcg32
member.summary: PCG32 — a small, fast, deterministic pseudo-random generator.

remarks.para: Neither engine gives you a usable deterministic RNG out of the box. Unity's UnityEngine.Random is a single global with hidden state that the engine itself draws from (particle systems and some built-in effects advance it), so a seeded run is not reproducible in practice. Unreal's FRandomStream is genuinely seedable and much closer to correct, but it is a plain LCG whose low bits are weak and whose stream is tied to the engine version.

So a game that needs reproducible worlds, replayable runs or a "share this seed" feature owns its generator. This is the same PCG32 as gamedev/engine/rng.py and produces the identical stream, verified against the reference implementation's published test vectors.
Everything is arithmetic, which wraps silently in C# by default — exactly the behaviour PCG needs.

member.name: T:GameCore.Tiles.TileGrid
member.summary: A rectangular grid of tile ids, with the broadphase that makes it useful.

remarks.para: Both engines have their own tilemap: Unity's Tilemap plus TilemapCollider2D, and Unreal's Paper2D tile maps. Those own rendering and physics colliders, which is work worth delegating. What they do not own is your gameplay's view of the level — line of sight, spawn rules, pathfinding, "is this tile safe to stand on" — and routing every one of those questions through the engine's collider system is both slow and untestable outside play mode. Keeping an authoritative grid in the core and treating the engine's tilemap as a rendering mirror is the pattern.

The rule that matters: never iterate the whole map. A 200x60 level is 12 000 tiles; testing an entity against all of them, sixty times a second, per entity, is the difference between a game and a slideshow. Because it is a grid, the tiles an entity could possibly touch are found by dividing its bounds by the tile size, so costs what the entity is big, not what the level is big.

Coordinate convention: row 0 is the bottom of the world, matching Unity's Y-up 2D space, so tile (x, y) sits at world (x * TileSize, y * TileSize) with no flip anywhere in the maths. ASCII levels are authored the way they look — first line is the top of the screen — and reverses them on load. Doing the flip once, at the authoring boundary, is what keeps sign errors out of the gameplay code. The Python original used Y-down throughout because it drew straight into a framebuffer; that is exactly the assumption that does not survive a port.

member.name: T:GameCore.Time.FixedTimestepAccumulator
member.summary: Converts elapsed wall-clock time into whole fixed-size simulation ticks.

remarks.para: Unity already does this for you and Unreal does not, which is the single most important scheduling difference between the two engines.

In Unity, FixedUpdate is driven by exactly this algorithm: real time accumulates, whole Time.fixedDeltaTime steps are drained out, and Time.maximumDeltaTime (0.333 s by default) is the clamp that stops the spiral of death. So in Unity you should put deterministic gameplay in FixedUpdate and never re-implement this — but you do need to know it exists, because it explains why input read in FixedUpdate misses button presses (a tick can run zero or twice in a frame) and why Update is the correct place to sample input.

In Unreal there is no gameplay equivalent. AActor::Tick receives a variable DeltaSeconds, and the fixed-step machinery (bSubstepping) applies to the physics solver only, not to your gameplay code. If you want reproducible gameplay in Unreal — for replays, deterministic tests, or lockstep networking — you accumulate DeltaSeconds yourself and step your simulation, which is precisely what this class is for.
This is a direct port of the Python implementation in gamedev/engine/loop.py, including the snap tolerance, which was found by a failing test rather than by reading about it.

member.name: F:GameCore.Time.FixedTimestepAccumulator.SnapTolerance
member.summary: How close to a whole tick the accumulator must be before it counts as whole.
member.remarks: Frame times are floats and essentially never land exactly on tick boundaries. A 30 Hz display against a 60 Hz tick should yield exactly two ticks per frame, but thirty frames of 1/30 s sum to 0.9999999999999999 s — 59.99999 ticks, which floors to 59. The missing tick surfaces as a one-frame hitch every few seconds: the class of bug reported as "it feels bad" and very hard to find. Snapping within a microsecond lets a tick run at most 1 us early, which is 0.006% of a 60 Hz tick, and makes integer-ratio refresh rates exact.
